questions.q: According to this lesson, what three operations does almost every ticketing REST API expose as the core pattern?
options: Create a case, update fields on an existing case, and add a comment to a case's timeline
Login, logout, and password reset
Export, import, and delete all cases
Only reading cases — creation always happens through the UI, never the API
questions.explain: Create, update, and comment form the generic pattern the lesson builds around, regardless of which specific ticketing product a team uses.

questions.q: What is the purpose of storing the alert's event_id in an external_ref field on the created ticket?
options: It is required by HTTP and has no functional purpose
It automatically deletes the ticket after 24 hours
It encrypts the ticket's description field
It lets the automation find the same ticket again later without keeping its own separate database of alert-to-ticket mappings
questions.explain: external_ref ties the ticket back to the originating alert, so a later lookup by event_id can find the existing ticket instead of creating a duplicate.

questions.q: Why does create_or_update_ticket() search for an existing open ticket by external_ref before calling create_ticket()?
options: Because the ticketing API requires a search call before every create call
To avoid opening a duplicate ticket when the same underlying alert recurs or is reprocessed
To delete any ticket that already exists for that alert
Searching has no effect on the outcome; it's purely optional logging
questions.explain: This is the same idempotency instinct from the webhook lesson applied one layer up: dedupe before creating, so recurring or retried alerts don't flood the queue with duplicate cases.

questions.q: Why does the lesson keep add_comment() and escalate_ticket() as two separate functions rather than one combined function?
options: The ticketing API technically forbids combining a comment and a field update in any way
Comments and field updates always use the same HTTP method, so splitting them saves no complexity
Separate functions let routine context (like an enrichment result) be logged without touching the ticket's status, while only a genuinely more severe signal changes status or priority
It has no real benefit; the lesson does this purely for code style
questions.explain: Keeping them separate lets an audit-trail comment get added without accidentally re-triggering an escalation, and vice versa.

questions.q: In the severity-to-priority mapping shown in this lesson, what does the mapping translate?
options: The ticketing system's priority field into the alert's severity field
An alert's timestamp into a ticket due date
The analyst's name into a ticket assignee ID
A security tool's severity scale (critical/high/medium/low) into the ticketing system's own priority scale (e.g. P1-P4)
questions.explain: severity_to_priority converts the alert's own severity label into whatever priority values the ticketing tool expects, so critical findings don't land in a queue sorted only by creation time.
